job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed the text as pasted, without checking it against the official engrossed version or existing law, so verify any cross-references to the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) and similar statutes before they go into talking points or amendments.

## Section 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton test applies to "a single vessel," so an operator can split recovery across several vessels or affiliates, each under the line. The text doesn't aggregate fleets, charterers, or commonly controlled entities.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" and measurement.** The text doesn't say whether "per year" means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or a rolling 12 months, or whether tonnage is wet or dry. Nodules carry substantial moisture, so the answer can change whether a vessel is over or under the threshold.

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "seabed."** Neither term is defined. It's unclear whether recovery means collecting on the seafloor or lifting to the surface, and whether "seabed" includes the subsoil. Both gaps invite disputes over when and where the threshold is crossed.

4. **§2(1)(A), the 200-meter depth test.** The text doesn't say what the depth is measured from or whether the test applies at the point of collection. It also isn't tied to any jurisdictional zone, so it sweeps in continental shelf slopes and areas within other nations' EEZs, not only the deep ocean.

5. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources."** Read literally, this could reach deepwater oil and gas, sand and gravel, and other non-nodule activity. That overbreadth could be used to build opposition from other industries and supports a vagueness challenge.

6. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's determination.** "The Secretary" is never defined (Commerce, Interior, State?), and "comparable" risk has no standard, procedure, or notice requirement. Because §5(b) attaches criminal liability to §3, this invites fair-notice, vagueness, and nondelegation challenges.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition omits foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, partnerships, LLCs, other unincorporated entities, permanent residents, and entities organized in D.C. or the territories. There is no ownership or control test, so a foreign-incorporated affiliate can do what its U.S. parent cannot.

8. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000-gross-ton floor and "equipped for the recovery" are both undefined or loose. A smaller vessel could mine commercially and stay out of the registry, while unrelated large vessels such as research ships and dredgers might be swept in. Modular equipment that is installed and removed also muddies "equipped."

## Section 3: Prohibition

9. **§3(a), "person in the United States."** Neither "person" nor "United States" is defined, so it's unclear whether this reaches the territorial sea, EEZ, or OCS. Because the hook is the person's location, not the activity's location, a foreign entity with no U.S. presence is outside it.

10. **§3(a), extraterritorial reach.** Applying the ban to U.S. persons "anywhere" invites challenge where they operate under another state's license or in its EEZ. It also leaves enforcement impractical absent vessel boarding authority or flag-state cooperation.

11. **§3(a), no ancillary prohibitions.** Nothing bars financing, offtake, onshore processing, equipment supply, transport, import of foreign-mined nodules, or aiding and abetting. Value-chain activity continues, and foreign-mined material can still enter U.S. supply chains.

12. **§3(a), subthreshold activity.** Only "commercial" mining is banned, so test mining, pilot collection, and exploration-scale recovery under 10,000 tons per vessel per year remain lawful.

13. **§3(b), "exploration license" is undefined.** The text doesn't say who issued it. A license from another country or an ISA-sponsoring state could qualify, and a license issued in the weeks before enactment would too.

14. **§3(b), mining "under" an exploration license.** Exploration licenses (for example under DSHMRA) don't ordinarily authorize commercial recovery, so the grandfathering is internally confusing. There is also no cap on tonnage, area, or duration, and nothing on renewals, extensions, modifications, transfers, or assignments. Holders of commercial recovery permits are not mentioned, which leaves a gap on the other side.

15. **§3(b), no relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or reference DSHMRA or OCSLA, so it's unclear whether permitting authority survives alongside the ban or is impliedly repealed. That is a ready-made litigation issue.

16. **§3(b), takings and due process.** Licensees not covered by the exemption, including pending applicants and permit holders, have no transition, compensation, or wind-down provision. This invites Fifth Amendment and reliance-based challenges.

17. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** It turns on the "purpose" of the activity, with no definition, quantity limit, duration limit, or government approval requirement. Large-scale "assessment" collection, and sale of what's recovered, could proceed under that label, and purpose is difficult to prove.

## Section 4: Registry

18. **§4(a), "operator."** The term is undefined, so owner/charterer/contractor structures create room to dodge. There is also no registration deadline.

19. **§4, no enforcement hook.** The §5 penalties attach only to violations of §3, so failing to register or file a report carries no stated penalty. Only general false-statement law (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §1001) might apply.

20. **§4(b), reporting content and verification.** "Describing the recovery activities" doesn't require tonnage, location, or disposition of material. The bill has no audit, inspection, observer, or tracking authority (e.g., AIS), so the self-certified reports can't be verified. The first due date also isn't specified.

21. **§4, no implementing authority.** There is no rulemaking direction to NOAA, no appropriation, and no public-disclosure provision. NOAA may lack both the mandate and the resources.

22. **§4 vs. §2(3), scope mismatch.** The registry covers only vessels over 5,000 GT, but the ban's threshold is tonnage-based and vessel-size-neutral, so the data captured doesn't line up with what's prohibited.

## Section 5: Penalties

23. **§5(a), no designated enforcer or process.** The section doesn't say who assesses or collects the penalty, what notice and hearing rights apply, or whether judicial review is available. It also gives the Attorney General no civil action or injunctive authority.

24. **§5(a), no seizure or forfeiture.** There is no authority to seize or forfeit vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals, and no Coast Guard role. The deterrent is weaker than it looks.

25. **§5(a), daily penalty mechanics.** Because the violation depends on an annual tonnage threshold, it's unclear which "day" the violation occurs on or whether it's continuing. A penalty of up to $1,000,000 per day also invites Excessive Fines challenges, and it isn't inflation-indexed.

26. **§5(a) vs. §8, retroactivity conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. That creates a fair-notice problem, an ex post facto argument on the criminal side, and an ambiguity over whether the 180-day gap is enforceable at all.

27. **§5(b), "willfully."** The mens rea is undefined. Combined with the open-ended Secretary determination in §2(1)(B), defendants can argue they lacked knowledge that the conduct was unlawful.

28. **§5, entity and individual liability.** The section has nothing on corporate officers, parent liability, or successor liability. Using shell or foreign-incorporated entities blunts enforcement.

## Sections 6–8: International agreement, duration, effective date

29. **§6, hortatory.** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to conclude anything, "equivalent" is undefined, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence for missing the 18 months. It's also unclear whether the 18 months is a deadline to begin negotiating or to finish.

30. **§7(a), lifting mechanism.** The text doesn't require anyone to commission or fund the National Academies report, set a timeline, or define "serious harm." A joint resolution also requires presidential signature, and it's unclear whether such a finding automatically ends the prohibition or whether partial findings (by area or technology) are permitted.

31. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), conflict.** One subsection makes the ban indefinite until a finding, the other ends the Act after 10 years regardless. Which controls is ambiguous, and as written the ban is temporary in any case.

32. **§7(b), sunset consequences.** There is no savings clause for violations committed before the sunset, so defendants may argue pending enforcement lapses. The grandfathering and registry also lapse, and the 10-year clock runs from enactment, so the effective prohibition is roughly 9.5 years.

33. **§8, 180-day gap.** Operators can expand or start activity during the gap and then claim reliance when the ban takes effect. There is no wind-down or transition rule for operations in progress, which invites emergency injunctive relief.

## Cross-cutting

34. **No findings or purpose section.** Without findings, the bill has a thinner record for defending the Commerce Clause basis and its extraterritorial scope.

35. **No severability clause.** If a provision such as §2(1)(B) or the extraterritorial reach is struck down, nothing says the rest survives.

36. **No agency allocation or regulatory framework.** The bill doesn't identify the lead enforcement agency and gives no rulemaking mandate, funding, or interagency coordination (NOAA, State, Coast Guard, DOJ), which makes consistent implementation hard.

37. **No citizen suit, whistleblower, or recordkeeping provisions.** Detecting and proving violations at sea depends entirely on self-reporting.

The items most likely to draw attention are 6 (Secretary's open-ended determination), 26 (the §5(a)/§8 retroactivity conflict), 31 (the §7(a)/§7(b) conflict), 5 (overbreadth to oil and gas and dredging), and 14–16 (grandfathering and takings).
